label: Establishing vs deploying vs maintaining a secure baseline

mentor.diagnosis: You treated the baseline as a document that gets written once. The objectives name three separate activities because the failure is almost always in the third one.
contrast: Decide the required configuration, from a benchmark such as CIS or a vendor guide, adapted to your environment
Copied verbatim without testing, so it breaks production
Push it to every in-scope system, through Group Policy, MDM or configuration management
Applied to the systems you knew about, missing the ones you did not
Detect drift, re-apply, and revise the baseline as threats and software change
Nobody checks, so the baseline describes a state that stopped existing months ago
mentor.rule: A baseline is a continuous control, not an artefact. If nothing detects drift from it, you have a document rather than a baseline.
mentor.tell: A stem where the configuration was correct at build time and is not correct now, or where new systems were built outside the process.
mentor.trap: Deploying is the visible work and maintaining is where the security actually lives. Drift detection is the control the exam expects you to name.

label: What hardening means for a server, a switch, cloud infrastructure, and a device you cannot patch

mentor.diagnosis: You applied the workstation answer to every device class. The exam separates them because some classes cannot take the standard answer at all.
contrast: Patch, remove roles and software, host firewall, endpoint protection, disable unused accounts
None, this is the default answer
Disable unused ports and services, change defaults, secure management plane, use out-of-band management
Treating the data plane and the management plane as one problem
Identity and policy configuration, least privilege, logging, no public exposure by default
Looking for a host to patch when the exposure is a misconfigured permission
MDM policy, encryption, screen lock, remote wipe, restrict sideloading
Segmentation, strict access control, monitoring, because patching is often impossible
Answering 'apply the patch' when no patch exists or downtime is unacceptable
mentor.rule: If the device class cannot be patched or rebooted, the answer is a compensating control: segment it, restrict who can reach it, and watch it closely.
mentor.tell: Operational technology, a production line, a medical device, a vendor who ended support, or a system that cannot be taken offline.
mentor.trap: Patch management is the correct answer so often that people pick it for the one class where it is specifically not available. Read for whether patching is even possible.

mentor.diagnosis: You sorted these by how much the employee likes them. The axis that matters is who owns the device, because ownership decides what the organisation may enforce and wipe.
contrast: Least: usually containerisation, and wiping only the corporate container
Most: full management, with personal use permitted
The employee, from an approved list
High: corporate ownership with some choice
mentor.rule: Ownership decides authority. If the employee owns the device you cannot wipe it wholesale, which is why BYOD drives containerisation and why the hardest questions are about privacy and legal exposure rather than technology.
mentor.tell: A stem about remote wiping a departing employee's phone, or about which model gives the most control.
mentor.trap: COPE and CYOD are both corporate-owned and differ only in who picked the hardware. The distinction people get wrong is CYOD against BYOD, because choice is confused with ownership.

label: Input validation vs static code analysis vs code signing vs sandboxing

mentor.diagnosis: You picked the technique that sounded most thorough rather than the one that acts at the moment described. Each operates at a different point in the life of the code.
contrast: Before the code runs, in the repository or build
Flaws visible in the source, without executing it
That data entering the application conforms before it is used
At publication, verified at install or load
Origin and integrity: this came from who it claims, unmodified
Containment: if it misbehaves, the damage is bounded
mentor.rule: Static analysis finds the flaw, input validation stops the payload, code signing proves the provenance, sandboxing limits the blast radius. Only one of them is about trusting where software came from.
mentor.tell: A stem about an application accepting malicious input points to validation. One about verifying a vendor's update points to signing. One about running an untrusted file safely points to sandboxing.
mentor.trap: Code signing proves origin and integrity and says nothing about whether the code is safe. Signed malware is signed, and the signature is doing its job.
